transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-12-09
- Start: 16:00 PST
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ruiz (CTO, Chemora), Markus Lee (ML Engineer), Priya Singh (Platform Engineer)

Optional sections:
Summary: See metadata summary above.
Topics: Hosted v Dedicated v Private, SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy, quotas, observability.
Action items: listed in metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Elena: Yes, loud and clear. Thanks, Jordan.
[00:06] Jordan: Great. Quick intros, I'm Jordan Park - account lead at Redwood, Samir is our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Samir: Hey all.
[00:13] Elena: I’m Elena, CTO at Chemora. Markus is our ML lead, Priya is on platform — we wanted to run through integration options.
[00:21] Markus: Hi.
[00:23] Priya: Hi.

[00:28] Jordan: Awesome. High-level, tell us what you're trying to build and what constraints you have.
[00:33] Elena: Sure. We're building a clinical insights assistant for internal research teams. There will be PHI-adjacent notes; some data will be de-identified but we still have strict compliance — SOC2 is baseline, we may need private or VPC options. Latency is important for interactive sessions — target sub 400ms for typical prompts. Cost is also a concern because we'll do a lot of batch embeddings for search.
[01:00] Jordan: Understood. When you say PHI-adjacent, is that going to be stored long-term in Redwood or do you need customer-managed keys and strict data residency?
[01:09] Elena: Prefer not to ship raw PHI. For any private info we'd like to keep it in our systems; we want request-level audit logs and KMS integration if possible.
[01:19] Samir: That aligns with Redwood Private / dedicated territory. Private gives a customer-managed control plane with KMS, audit logs, and on-prem options. Dedicated gives isolation and committed capacity but still uses Redwood-managed control plane. For quick validation, many customers try hosted first and then move to Dedicated or Private for compliance.
[01:36] Markus: Does your hosted API offer an option to not persist prompts? Like opt-out of retention?
[01:42] Jordan: Yes, we have retention controls and an enterprise setting to disable retention and turn on request-level logging; we can provide SOC2 docs and the retention policy — I'll share that after the call.

[01:53] Priya: From a networking view: we would prefer VPC peering, private link — we can’t open wide internet egress from our cluster. Does Redwood support VPC peering for Dedicated?
[02:03] Samir: Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private supports full VPC control plane. For hosted, we offer region-level compliance but not peering. We can map out options — dedicated often hits the middle ground.

[02:15] Elena: On the integration surface, our engineers use LangChain + LlamaIndex heavily. Do you have SDKs or first-class examples?
[02:22] Samir: Yes. We have Python and Typescript SDKs, with connectors for LangChain and a LlamaIndex sample. Our SDKs include streaming, function calling primitives, and embedding helpers. I'll share a repo with LangChain + RAG examples.
[02:35] Markus: For LlamaIndex, what’s the workflow? Do you recommend pushing embeddings into our vector DB or using Redwood embeddings service?
[02:42] Samir: You can do both. Many customers compute embeddings via Redwood to take advantage of batching and lower unit cost, then index in your DB. Alternatively, you can fetch embeddings from Redwood on demand. If you want to offload compute we can batch embeddings and return them for your index.
[02:57] Markus: Okay. Latency during chat is more critical than embedding throughput. How does batching affect tail latency?
[03:03] Samir: Good question. We balance batching with latency SLOs; our runtime does continuous batching and can be tuned per endpoint. For interactive chat, set a low batch timeout and smaller max batch size. For embeddings, larger batches are better to improve throughput.

[03:18] Priya: What about a gateway/proxy pattern — we have an internal proxy that enforces rate limits, request tagging, per-team quotas. Can Redwood sit behind our gateway or do you expect clients to call you directly?
[03:30] Jordan: Both are supported. We often see a small on-prem or sidecar gateway for routing and auth, or customers call Redwood directly from their backend. Some customers use a lightweight proxy to handle quota enforcement and observability tags before calling Redwood.
[03:42] Priya: Any recommended headers we should propagate for tracing and request attribution?
[03:46] Samir: We accept standard traceparent and baggage headers for W3C tracing. We also support x-redwood-tenant and x-redwood-request-id for attribution; plus you can pass metadata fields in the SDK for per-request tags.

[03:57] Markus: If we front a proxy, how do rate limits apply? Are they per-API-key or per-IP?
[04:02] Samir: Rate limits are per API key/tenant. If you front a single API key through your proxy you'll hit the aggregate limits for that key. We recommend issuing per-service keys or using per-team keys and rotating them; we also have quota enforcement in the console so you can partition usage.

[04:17] Elena: We're also curious about observability — we need token-level cost reports, latency histograms, and per-route error tracing integrated with our existing stack (Datadog).
[04:27] Samir: Console exports metrics and we have a tracing hook for sending spans to OTLP-compatible collectors. For token-level costs we provide per-request billing metadata; you can export usage to S3 or via API for ingestion into Datadog.

[04:40] Priya: Do you have webhook callbacks for async jobs — e.g., embedding batches finish and we want a callback?
[04:45] Samir: Yes, we support async jobs with callbacks and a polling endpoint. We can also push to a customer-owned queue; we'll share the job API docs.

[04:54] Jordan: Let's dig into sample architecture — Samir, maybe you can sketch how a LangChain RAG setup looks with a proxy.
[04:59] Samir: Sure. (typing) Imagine an internal API gateway that validates SSO headers and enforces rate limiting per team. The gateway sends segmented requests to Redwood — either via per-team keys or through a service account that includes a team-tag header. For embeddings, clients call Redwood's embeddings endpoint with batch size tuned to your throughput. The vector DB stays in your VPC. For private deployments, the calling is inside your network so the data never leaves.
[05:26] Markus: For a private deployment, what's the typical lead time? We have a compliance review by end of Q1 2028.
[05:33] Samir: Private on-prem can vary — typically 6–12 weeks for initial deployment depending on infra readiness. Dedicated (reserved capacity) can be much quicker — 2–4 weeks. Hosted is immediate.

[05:44] Elena: Cost wise, for dedicated, do we still pay per-token or do you switch to committed GPU hours?
[05:50] Jordan: Dedicated is committed capacity pricing: you reserve GPU pools and get predictable throughput, which is helpful for bursty workloads and steady cost plans. There are usage tiers that include model execution credits; we'll send a pricing sheet.

[06:02] Priya: Any guidance on quantization or model variants to reduce cost without changing behavior?
[06:07] Samir: We recommend evaluated quantized variants on a small eval set. For Llama-style models, 8-bit or 4-bit quantization can reduce cost substantially with minimal regressions for many tasks. Redwood Optimize can suggest a profile based on your prompt distribution.

[06:19] Elena: On security, we need to know SAML SSO for access to console, RBAC for routes, and audit log retention (minimum 1 year).
[06:29] Jordan: We support SAML/SSO and granular RBAC. Audit logs are configurable - 1 year retention can be arranged under enterprise terms. I'll attach the security pack.

[06:39] Markus: A couple of technical nitty-gritty: does SDK support streaming tokens with cancellation? We might need to cancel long-running calls from the client.
[06:46] Samir: SDK supports streaming with backpressure and cancellation tokens in both Python and TS. We also expose a token-level progress callback.

[06:56] Priya: Any limits on number of concurrent streaming sessions? We expect a few hundred concurrent interactive users at peak.
[07:02] Samir: Concurrent sessions map to throughput and reserved capacity. For hosted, concurrency is subject to rate limits per key; for dedicated we size pools accordingly. We can run a spike test during the pilot.

[07:12] Jordan: Speaking of testing, would you be open to a 2-week pilot with a small dataset and scripted load?
[07:18] Elena: Yes, that's ideal. We want a pilot that exercises chat latency, embeddings throughput, and end-to-end tracing with our proxy.

[07:24] Markus: For the pilot we'll want to validate: 1) chat latency <400ms median on target payloads, 2) embedding throughput target of X reqs/min (we'll provide exact numbers), 3) no retention of raw PHI in hosted unless we explicitly enable it.
[07:39] Samir: Sounds good. We'll help design the benchmark and provide SDKs and configs for batch/latency tradeoffs.

[07:45] Elena: One more—team wants to integrate with LlamaIndex and test retrieval augmentation. Any gotchas?
[07:50] Samir: Main consideration is embedding consistency and tokenization differences. We'll supply an example showing LlamaIndex doc loaders using Redwood embeddings, and show how to persist metadata for traceability. Also a pointer on how to stream partial RAG responses.

[07:59] Priya: Regarding quotas, how do you prevent noisy neighbors if we give multiple teams keys?
[08:05] Samir: You can set per-key hard quotas and per-route rate caps; our console supports quota templates so platform can programmatically create and assign quotas. We also have alerting for quota breaches.

[08:16] Jordan: Competition question — do you currently evaluate any other vendors?
[08:19] Elena: We ran some initial PoCs with Anthropic and a small internal OpenAI integration. Cost/time-to-deploy were differentiators. Cohere was mentioned for embeddings but their latency profile was less ideal.

[08:30] Jordan: Good to know. We'll highlight where Redwood helps on latency controls, dedicated capacity, and observability during the follow-up.

[08:36] Markus: Could you also show examples of using your SDK from within a Kubernetes sidecar or a Lambda? We expect a mix of serverless and k8s workloads.
[08:46] Samir: Yes — we have patterns for sidecars (rate limiting, batching at the sidecar) and for ephemeral serverless clients with short-lived keys. I'll include both examples.

[08:56] Priya: Are there pre-built integrations with Datadog and Sentry for error tracing?
[08:59] Samir: We have Datadog exporters and OTLP-compatible traces that you can ingest into Sentry. We'll include a sample OTLP collector config.

[09:08] Elena: Timeline-wise, our procurement window is Jan 2028. If we start a pilot this month, we can align decisions in January.
[09:16] Jordan: That's doable. We'll prioritize the security pack and pricing to fit your procurement timelines.

[09:22] Markus: Small note — our prompts include medical shorthand and some OCR noise. Will Redwood's tokenization or models handle that, or should we normalize prior to sending?
[09:32] Samir: Normalization helps. We can also run a short quality eval with your prompt set and show regressions across model variants. Redwood Optimize can recommend preprocessing heuristics too.

[09:44] Elena: Great. Anything else from your side?
[09:46] Jordan: Just to confirm next steps — we'll send the pricing/security docs, SDK samples including LangChain and LlamaIndex, and propose a pilot plan.
[09:55] Priya: Sounds good. Also, we'll share our network diagram and example traffic profile.

[10:00] Jordan: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invites for a pilot kickoff and a spike test plan. Thanks everyone.
[10:06] Elena: Thank you.
[10:07] Jordan: Bye.
